chunks: Ground probes and ground test points. The question: What are ground probes on a PCB? Why are they needed? When should they be used?
A ground probe point is a pad on the board connected to the ground plane, placed right next to a signal test point.
A scope (oscilloscope, which draws voltage against time) measures the voltage between its probe tip and its ground clip, so a fast signal is only measured well if that ground connection is short.
A nearby ground pad lets you use a very short ground path.
Imagine measuring how a ball bounces using a long, floppy measuring stick. If the stick itself swings, you measure the stick's wobble as well as the ball.
A long ground lead is that floppy stick: it wobbles, and it also picks up stray noise like an antenna. A short connection to the ground pad is a stiff ruler.
The probe's input capacitance C in is charged through the ground lead's inductance L gnd (orange).
A fast edge excites a series LC resonance, f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) about 130 megahertz for 150 nanohenries and 10 picofarads.
The scope displays V scope, the voltage across C in, so it shows this ring even though the circuit doesn't have it.
Ground pad: a pad tied straight to the ground plane through vias (small plated holes), for connecting the probe's return.
Return path: the route the signal's current takes back to ground, which forms a loop with the signal. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current.
A longer wire has more. Ringing: a signal wobbling back and forth after a fast edge. Ground plane: a large copper layer used as the common reference.
A 15 cm clip lead has roughly 150 nanohenries of inductance.

Together with the probe's 10 picofarads of input capacitance (its small built-in charge storage), it rings at about 130 megahertz, so a fast edge shows overshoot (the signal swinging past its true level) that is not really on the board.
A short ground spring of about 10 nanohenries rings near 500 megahertz, much further from the signal's content. The loop is also smaller, so it picks up less noise.
That is the whole idea.
"A ground probe point is a pad tied to the ground plane through vias, placed right beside a signal test point so a scope's ground can attach with a very short loop.
It's needed because a probe measures tip minus ground, and a long ground lead adds inductance that rings with the probe capacitance and picks up noise.
I use them next to any fast or sensitive test point and power rail. In fixtures, ground probes serve the same role for the tester's reference."
